transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess I’m here because I can’t get past how I look. It’s mostly my hairline and my face, especially at work under those restaurant lights. I’m a host, so I’m right up front, and I keep feeling like I look old or… strange somehow.

People I work with say they don’t see it, or they tell me I look fine, but I don’t know. The lighting there is brutal—like those overhead bulbs make every angle worse. I’ll be trying to seat people and I’m thinking about whether they’re staring at my forehead or my face instead of just doing my job. So… yeah, that’s why I came in.
Do you find yourself feeling self-conscious about other parts of your body, or is it mainly your hairline and face that bother you?

It’s mainly the hairline and my face, yeah. I mean, I’ll notice other things sometimes, but the thing I can’t stop circling back to is that under the restaurant lights, I look old and kind of strange. Like my forehead and face just look… off.

And it’s annoying because my coworkers will say, “I don’t see what you’re talking about,” but then I’m standing there at the host stand thinking, well, maybe they’re just being nice. Those lights make everyone look bad, honestly—there’s this one table near the front where the glare hits the menu covers too—but for me it’s like I can’t stop thinking people are seeing what I’m seeing.
When you’re upset about how your hairline or face looks, do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, touching your face, or trying to cover it up?

Yeah… I do. Probably more than I want to admit.

Before a shift, I’ll get stuck in the bathroom checking the mirror over and over, like from straight on and then the side, and then I’ll take pictures on my phone from different angles because somehow the mirror doesn’t feel “true,” if that makes sense. And then the phone pictures make it worse, usually.

I’ll keep combing my hair forward, trying to get the hairline to look less obvious. Sometimes I’m doing that while I’m thinking about how the guests are going to see me when I’m at the host stand. Like, if the light hits me from above, or if someone’s sitting lower and looking up at me—sorry, that probably sounds ridiculous. There’s this one light near the front that makes everyone look washed out, and I notice it every time I walk past it.

But yeah, I’ll get caught up doing all that until I’m late coming out, or I’m so worked up I don’t even want to go to the front.
Does this concern about how your face and hairline look cause you a lot of distress, or make it hard for you to do things like work or spend time with others?

Yeah… it’s gotten in the way a lot. I mean, more than just “I feel bad about it.”

At the restaurant, I’ve been written up because I’ll be late coming out to the host stand, or I’ll miss shifts when I just can’t face being under those lights and having people look at me. And the manager tries to be polite, but you can tell they’re annoyed, because it’s a restaurant and everybody has to show up on time—especially up front.

And outside work too… I’ve stopped going to staff photos, because I can’t stand the idea of my face being captured like that. I used to go to gallery events sometimes—there’s this little place downtown that does openings, and I liked the free wine and just wandering around—but now I’ll think about how I’ll look in the lighting or if someone takes a picture. Same with hikes. I know that sounds unrelated, but people always take photos on hikes, and then the sun hits your forehead a certain way, and… yeah, I just don’t go.

So yes. It’s affecting work and being around people. A lot.
Can you tell me how long you’ve felt this way about your hairline and face? Has it been something that’s bothered you every day, most days, or only occasionally?

I don’t know if I can put an exact date on it. It’s not like I woke up one Tuesday and suddenly thought it. It’s more that… this is why I’m here, because I can’t stop thinking about my hairline and how my face looks, especially under the restaurant lights.

I’ll be standing there and it’s like, I look old, I look strange, something is off. And then coworkers say they don’t see it, but that doesn’t really make it go away. I just think maybe they’re being polite or they’re not looking the way I’m looking.

So, yeah, it’s not really occasional. It feels like it’s there a lot, especially when I’m at work or thinking about being seen.
Do you think the issue with your hairline and face is something that most people would notice, or do you think it’s something that only you notice or worry about?

I mean… I know people say they don’t notice it. My coworkers will tell me, “You look fine,” or they don’t see what I’m talking about, and I get that maybe from their side it isn’t obvious.

But to me it feels really obvious. Like under the restaurant lights, especially those bright overhead ones, I can’t stop thinking my hairline and my face make me look old or strange. It’s hard to believe other people aren’t seeing it too, even if they say they aren’t.

And then I start thinking about how customers are looking at me, or whether the lighting by the host stand is making it worse… sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess the answer is, logically maybe it’s mostly me worrying about it, but it feels like everyone can see it.
Do you believe that other people are noticing or judging this part of your appearance, even if they don’t mention it, or do you feel like it’s mostly your own concern?

I guess… it’s both, but it doesn’t feel like “mostly my own concern” when I’m standing there.

I’m here because I can’t stop thinking that my hairline, and the way my face looks under those restaurant lights, makes me look old and strange. And coworkers will say they don’t see what I’m talking about, and I try to take that in, but then I’m at the host stand and the lights are right overhead and I start thinking, no, they have to notice. Customers too.

It’s like when you’re in one of those dressing rooms with terrible lighting—actually, restaurants have kind of the same thing sometimes, all shiny surfaces and weird reflections—and you catch yourself from the side and it just ruins your whole… sorry. But yes, I do feel like people are noticing or judging it, even if they don’t say anything.
Do you find yourself worrying about other things besides your appearance, like feeling down, hopeless, or anxious about different parts of your life?

I’m not sure how to separate it, honestly. Like, if I’m anxious, it usually loops right back to the appearance thing, if that makes sense.

I mean, life stuff happens—work schedules, money, getting older, all of that—but I don’t know if I sit around worrying about those the same way. It’s more like I’ll start thinking about something normal, and then I catch my reflection in the glass by the bar, or I remember how the lights hit my face, and suddenly that’s where my head goes.

Feeling down… I don’t know. Maybe sometimes, but I couldn’t tell you if it’s separate from this. It’s hard to answer cleanly.

When you feel distressed about how you look, does it always center on your hairline and face, or do you also worry about other parts of your appearance or other things in your life during those moments?

Mostly it comes back to my hairline and my face. I mean, I can get distracted for a minute by other things, but when I’m really distressed about how I look, that’s the thing.

It’s like… I’m here because I can’t stop thinking about how my hairline looks, and how my face looks under the restaurant lights. Those overhead lights make everything look harsher, and then I feel like I look old or strange. Even when my coworkers tell me they don’t see what I’m talking about, I still can’t quite believe it.

Sometimes I’ll start thinking about something else at work, like where to seat people or whether the lounge is getting backed up, and then I catch the reflection in the glass or the brass by the host stand—sorry, the restaurant has all these reflective surfaces—and it just goes right back to that. My hairline, my face, the lighting. That’s what it centers on.
